screens.title: Mappings, Structs, and Arrays
screens.subtitle: Organizing on-chain data for lookup, grouping, and collection

narration.text: In this lesson we are going to build a clear mental model for three fundamental Solidity tools: mappings for fast key-value lookup, structs for grouping related fields into a single record, and arrays for ordered collections. You will see when each structure is the right choice and why combining them is the common pattern in production contracts. For example, a mapping from product ID to a Product struct gives you O(1) lookups while a separate dynamic array of IDs lets you iterate when needed. We will emphasize gas implications: writing to storage costs a lot, copies to memory are cheaper but ephemeral, and calldata is the most efficient for external read-only inputs. A short live-coding walkthrough uses the ProductCatalog and AssetTracker examples from the chapter so you can connect code to behavior. By the end of this module you should be able to choose a design pattern that balances lookup speed, iteration capability, and gas cost, and you will know a concrete way to avoid common pitfalls like attempting to iterate a mapping or deleting middle elements incorrectly. Ready to explore key patterns and a hands-on asset tracker example?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use mappings for efficient lookup, structs to model complex entities, and arrays when iteration or ordered lists are required — always consider storage vs memory costs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills that let you design on-chain data cleanly and efficiently. First, you will use mappings to store key-value pairs for fast lookups; for instance, mapping an address to a balance lets you check an account without looping. Second, you will define and use structs to group related fields into a single custom type; this lets you store product metadata as one object instead of scattered variables. Third, you will work with dynamic and fixed-size arrays, knowing when to use each and how operations like push, pop, and length affect gas and iteration. Finally, you will clearly distinguish between memory and storage data locations and manage their gas implications when passing arrays or structs into functions. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to anchor the idea and a verified competency milestone so you can self-check your progress. These skills are essential for building registries, asset trackers, and other DApps where reliability and gas efficiency matter.

First, implement a mapping from asset ID to an Asset struct so you can retrieve an asset immediately by its identifier. Second, create an array of asset IDs per owner so owners can list their assets; this pairs mapping for lookup with arrays for iteration. screens.title: Mappings — definition and simple usage
screens.subtitle: How mappings provide efficient key-value lookup

narration.text: A mapping is Solidity's built-in key-value store. Think of it as a dictionary where a key maps directly to a value on chain. The important claim is that mappings are optimized for direct lookup: given the key, reading or writing the value is efficient compared to scanning a list. For a concrete example, the chapter shows mapping from address to uint256 balances. This allows you to set and retrieve a user's balance with direct syntax that looks like an array access. A common misconception is expecting mappings to be iterable. Mappings do not store keys in a list and you cannot loop through them on-chain to discover all entries. If you need enumeration, pair a mapping with an array of keys or an array of structs that record IDs. Another important nuance: mapping values can themselves be mappings, structs, or arrays, enabling nested structures such as owner mapped to assets by name. In practice, you will use mappings for ownership lookups, token balances, and lookup tables. Takeaway: use mappings when you need fast, keyed access and do not need to enumerate keys on-chain. How will you pair a mapping with an iterable list when you need both behaviors?

keyIdea.title: Mapping takeaway
keyIdea.text: Mappings are ideal for fast lookups but not for enumeration; combine with arrays when iteration is required.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Mappings — definition and simple usage
Definition

mapping(Key => Value) VariableName

Mappings store key-value pairs. Keys are not enumerable, and lookups are efficient.

// mapping: address => uint256
mapping(address => uint256) public userBalances;

function setBalance(address _user, uint256 _amount) public {
    userBalances[_user] = _amount;
}

function getBalance(address _user) public view returns (uint256) {
    return userBalances[_user];
}
Example

Use a mapping to store balances so the contract can look up any address in constant time without scanning storage.

Common misconception

Attempting to iterate a mapping directly. You must record keys elsewhere if you need enumeration.

Visual
Mapping characteristics
  • Direct lookup by key.
  • Keys are not stored as an iterable list.
  • Values can be complex types.
  • Nested mappings allowed.
When to use

Ownership maps, registry tables, quick access patterns where iteration is not required on-chain.

Key Takeaway

Use mappings for fast, keyed access. If you need to list entries later, maintain an array of keys alongside the mapping.

screens.title: Nested mappings and limitations
screens.subtitle: Track complex relationships with nested keys and complementary arrays

narration.text: Nested mappings let you express two-dimensional relationships on chain. For example, mapping from owner address to mapping of asset name to quantity models per-owner holdings of named assets. The claim is that nested mappings preserve lookup efficiency while modeling hierarchical relations. Concretely, ownedAssets[owner][assetName] returns a quantity directly. A common mistake is relying on mappings for enumeration: nested mappings still do not expose keys. If you need to list all assets for an owner, maintain an array of asset names or IDs per owner. Another nuance is gas and storage complexity: nested mappings of dynamic keys are fine for lookup but can make cleanup or bulk operations expensive if you try to remove many entries in one transaction. A pattern in the chapter pairs nested mappings with arrays or structs that record IDs so you can iterate externally or in batched on-chain operations. Takeaway: use nested mappings for indexed, fast access and pair them with arrays or indexed events when you need discoverability or iteration. Nested mappings and limitations means nested mappings model owner-scoped or multi-key relationships; pair them with arrays when you need enumerable lists.. In practical terms, track complex relationships with nested keys and complementary arrays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Nested mapping pattern
keyIdea.text: Nested mappings model owner-scoped or multi-key relationships; pair them with arrays when you need enumerable lists.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Nested mappings and limitations
Definition & Example

mapping(address => mapping(string => uint256)) ownedAssets;

// Nested mapping example
mapping(address => mapping(string => uint256)) public ownedAssets;

function setAssetQuantity(address _owner, string memory _assetName, uint256 _quantity) public {
    ownedAssets[_owner][_assetName] = _quantity;
}

function getAssetQuantity(address _owner, string memory _assetName) public view returns (uint256) {
    return ownedAssets[_owner][_assetName];
}
When to use

Model per-owner collections keyed by a name or id, such as balances per asset per owner.

Pitfall

You cannot enumerate the second-level keys on-chain. Maintain a separate array if you need a list for the owner.

Design patterns
  • Use nested mappings for two-dimensional lookups like owner→asset→quantity.
  • Keep an owner-specific array of asset names to enable enumeration.
  • Emit events on updates so off-chain indexers can discover keys cheaply.
Key Takeaway

Nested mappings are powerful for scoped lookups but are not iterable. Pair them with arrays or events when discoverability matters.

screens.title: Structs — modeling complex entities
screens.subtitle: Group fields into coherent records like Product or Asset

narration.text: Structs let you create custom types by grouping several fields into one named record. This is useful whenever an entity has multiple attributes that belong together, such as id, name, price, seller, and availability in a product listing. The chapter demonstrates using a Product struct with a mapping from productId to Product. A concrete example shows adding a product, setting its fields, and storing it in the mapping. Be aware of storage semantics: when you retrieve a struct from a mapping using a storage reference, you get a pointer that modifies the state in place; using a memory copy leaves the original state unchanged. A common misconception is thinking a struct assignment always creates a copy; assignment to a storage variable from storage creates a reference, not a copy. Structs also help reduce the number of state variables and make accessors and return types more organized. Takeaway: use structs to model real-world entities on chain and be explicit about memory versus storage when manipulating them to avoid unintended state changes. Structs — modeling complex entities means structs simplify storage of grouped fields. when reading or writing, decide whether you need a storage reference or a memory copy.. In practical terms, group fields into coherent records like product or asset. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Struct takeaway
keyIdea.text: Structs simplify storage of grouped fields. When reading or writing, decide whether you need a storage reference or a memory copy.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Structs — modeling complex entities
Struct example

Product struct pattern

struct Product {
    uint256 id;
    string name;
    uint256 price;
    address seller;
    bool available;
}

mapping(uint256 => Product) public products;
uint256 public nextProductId = 0;

function addProduct(string memory _name, uint256 _price) public {
    Product storage newProduct = products[nextProductId];
    newProduct.id = nextProductId;
    newProduct.name = _name;
    newProduct.price = _price;
    newProduct.seller = msg.sender;
    newProduct.available = true;
    nextProductId++;
}
Example

Create a Product record and store it in a mapping so you can find product metadata by ID quickly.

Misconception

Assigning one storage struct to another creates a reference, not a deep copy. Use explicit copying to avoid accidental state changes.

Patterns & tips
  • Use storage for in-place updates to structs from mappings.
  • Use memory when you only need a temporary snapshot for calculations.
  • Keep a separate ID array when you must iterate over products.
Key Takeaway

Structs model complex entities. Be deliberate about storage vs memory to control when state changes occur.

screens.title: Arrays — fixed-size vs dynamic
screens.subtitle: Choose the right array type and understand operations and pitfalls

narration.text: Arrays hold ordered collections of elements of the same type. Solidity supports fixed-size arrays where length is set at compile time and dynamic arrays which can grow or shrink at runtime. A fixed-size array like five integers reserves a predictable amount of storage and is suitable when the number of elements is known in advance. Dynamic arrays are useful for lists that change — you can push new elements, pop the last element, and read length. The chapter warns about gas implications: iterating over large dynamic arrays in a single transaction can exceed gas limits and permit denial-of-service scenarios. Another common pitfall is deleting an element from the middle: the delete operation sets the element to its default value but does not shift others, leaving gaps. If you need to remove an element while keeping contiguous indices, use the swap-with-last technique and then pop the last element. The concrete example in the chapter shows keeping product IDs in a dynamic array to allow iteration of items; however, removal must be handled carefully to avoid expensive loops. Final takeaway: pick the array type based on expected operations and plan removal and iteration strategies with gas in mind.

keyIdea.title: Array takeaway
keyIdea.text: Fixed arrays for known-size data; dynamic arrays for changing lists. Avoid expensive full-array loops and use swap-and-pop for safe removals.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Arrays — fixed-size vs dynamic
Fixed-size

uint256[5] fixedNumbers;

Fixed arrays reserve space and cannot change length. Use when size is known and stable.

Dynamic

uint256[] dynamicNumbers;

Dynamic arrays support push, pop, and length, but operations that iterate all elements may be gas-heavy.

// Safe removal using swap and pop
function removeByIndex(uint256 index) internal {
    uint256 lastIndex = items.length - 1;
    if (index != lastIndex) {
        items[index] = items[lastIndex];
    }
    items.pop();
}
Common mistakes & advice
  • Avoid attempting to iterate very large arrays in one transaction.
  • Deleting sets defaults but leaves gaps; decide whether gaps are acceptable.
  • Use events and off-chain indexing to avoid on-chain enumeration when feasible.
Key Takeaway

Choose array type for expected operations. Use swap-and-pop for efficient removals and prefer batched or off-chain iteration when arrays grow large.

screens.title: Data locations: storage, memory, calldata
screens.subtitle: How data location affects behavior, cost, and mutability

narration.text: Data location determines where complex data lives and how assignments behave. Storage refers to the persistent state on the blockchain; state variables live here and writing to storage is the most expensive operation. Memory is temporary and exists only for the duration of a function call; when you pass a large array to an internal function as memory, a copy may be created, which costs gas but is cheaper than storage writes. Calldata is a read-only area for external function arguments; it is the cheapest for passing data from outside calls. Concretely, when you set Product storage p = products[id], p becomes a reference directly to the state entry and modifications change the stored struct. If you instead declare Product memory p = products[id], you get a copy you can modify locally without altering state. A frequent misconception is believing that passing a storage array into a function that expects memory will be free — it triggers a copy. The process to decide: if you need to persist changes, use storage; for read-only or temporary computations, use memory or calldata. Final thought: always be explicit with the data location keyword for function parameters of complex types to avoid surprising gas costs or bugs.

keyIdea.title: Location summary
keyIdea.text: storage persists and is expensive; memory is temporary and cheaper; calldata is cheapest for external read-only inputs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Data locations: storage, memory, calldata
Quick definitions
  • storage: persistent state, expensive to write.
  • memory: temporary per-call storage, cheaper, used for local copies.
  • calldata: external, read-only arguments, most gas efficient for external calls.
function processArrayInStorage() public {
    uint256[] storage myArr = storageArray; // reference, modifies state
    myArr.push(100);
}

function processArrayInMemory(uint256[] memory _inputArray) public pure returns (uint256) {
    uint256 sum = 0;
    for (uint i=0; i<_inputArray.length; i++) sum += _inputArray[i];
    return sum;
}
Deciding rule

If you intend to modify state and persist changes, use storage. If you only need temporary data for computation, use memory. For external read-only parameters prefer calldata.

Misconception

Passing storage variables to functions expecting memory will create a copy and cost gas; be mindful of implicit copying.

Key Takeaway

Be explicit with data location keywords for complex types in function signatures to control gas and semantics.

screens.title: AssetTracker walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Create and transfer assets using mapping, struct, and arrays

narration.text: The AssetTracker example in the chapter ties together mappings, structs, and arrays in a small contract you can implement in Remix. The contract defines an Asset struct with id, name, owner, and creation timestamp. Assets are stored in mapping from id to Asset, and each owner has an array of asset IDs. When creating an asset, the contract writes a new Asset into storage mapping and pushes the id into ownerAssets for the sender. The transfer function updates the owner field in the asset struct and pushes the id to the new owner’s array. A common simplification shown in the activity is not removing the id from the old owner's array to avoid the gas complexity of searching and deleting; in production you would implement swap-and-pop or an index map to support efficient removal. The walkthrough also highlights how events like AssetCreated and AssetTransferred allow off-chain systems to maintain accurate lists without expensive on-chain iterations. Takeaway: this contract is a practical pattern; it demonstrates mapping lookup by id, struct storage semantics, and array-based owner listings while teaching trade-offs about tidy removals versus gas cost.

keyIdea.title: AssetTracker pattern
keyIdea.text: Store assets in a mapping by id, keep per-owner arrays of ids for listing, and use events for off-chain indexing; handle removals thoughtfully for gas.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › AssetTracker walkthrough
Asset struct
struct Asset {
    uint256 id;
    string name;
    address owner;
    uint256 creationTimestamp;
}

mapping(uint256 => Asset) public assets;
mapping(address => uint256[]) public ownerAssets;
uint256 public nextAssetId = 0;
Create flow

Create Asset in storage and push id into ownerAssets for the creator. Emit AssetCreated event for off-chain indexing.

Transfer flow

Update the owner in the asset struct, push id to new owner's array, emit AssetTransferred. Removing id from old owner is more complex and often avoided in simple demos.

Practical notes
  • Events let off-chain indexers maintain lists without on-chain enumeration.
  • When removing IDs from owner arrays, plan for swap-and-pop or an index map to avoid heavy loops.
  • Be explicit about storage when mutating the asset struct so changes persist.
Key Takeaway

AssetTracker unites mapping, struct, and arrays. Use events and careful removal strategies to balance correctness and gas.

screens.title: Combining patterns: mapping → struct → array
screens.subtitle: Architectural pattern for registries and catalogs

narration.text: A common architecture for registries and catalogs chains three elements: a mapping keyed by ID maps to a struct representing the entity, and a dynamic array holds IDs for iteration. The mapping provides efficient direct access to an entity, the struct groups related fields for clarity, and the ID array lets you produce lists for UI and batch operations. For example, ProductCatalog stores Product structs in a mapping keyed by productId and pushes productId into productIds array each time an item is added. The key trade-off is that mappings alone cannot be iterated, so you accept the cost of an extra array write to record keys. Another design choice is maintaining reverse indexes, such as a mapping from owner to array of IDs, which supports owner-scoped lists but increases the cost on create and transfer operations. A misconception is to duplicate all fields across structures for convenience — duplication increases gas and risk of inconsistency. Instead, keep a single source of truth in the mapping and use arrays and events for indexing and discovery. Ask yourself: where will iteration happen, on-chain or off-chain, and design the mix of mapping, struct, and array accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Pattern takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use mapping for truth, struct for modeling, and arrays for indexability. Minimize duplicated state to reduce gas and inconsistencies.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Combining patterns: mapping → struct → array
Architecture

Mapping stores truth • Struct models entity • Array indexes IDs

mapping(uint256 => Product) public products;
uint256[] public productIds;

function addProduct(...) {
    // create product in mapping
    productIds.push(nextProductId);
}
Design choice

Decide whether the array is maintained on-chain for on-chain listings or produced off-chain via events and indexes.

Trade-offs
  • Extra array writes cost gas but enable on-chain iteration.
  • Events can provide off-chain indexing at lower on-chain cost.
  • Avoid copying fields across structures to prevent inconsistency.
Key Takeaway

Design the mapping-struct-array trio around where iteration will happen and how often writes occur to balance cost and functionality.

screens.title: Gas pitfalls and safe removal patterns
screens.subtitle: Avoid iteration DoS and handle deletions correctly

narration.text: The chapter highlights several gas-related pitfalls you will likely encounter as data structures grow. Iterating over a large dynamic array in a single transaction can exceed gas limits and allow denial-of-service if user actions must process the whole list. To avoid this, design incremental or batched operations, or perform heavy listing off-chain using events. Deleting elements in the middle of an array is another frequent source of bugs: delete sets the element to its default value, leaving a gap. The recommended approach for removing an entry while preserving contiguity is swap the target with the last element and pop the last element. This is O(1) but reorders elements, so only use it when order is not important. Also be cautious about copying large storage arrays into memory for processing; large copies are expensive. A concrete tip is to maintain an index mapping from id to position in the owner array to make removals efficient. Lastly, duplicating state across mappings and arrays increases gas and complexity; prefer a single source of truth and use events or indexes to provide alternate views. Takeaway: anticipate growth and design removal, iteration, and indexing strategies with gas in mind.

keyIdea.title: Gas & deletion
keyIdea.text: Prevent DoS by avoiding full-array loops; use swap-and-pop or index maps to remove items efficiently and keep a single source of truth.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Gas pitfalls and safe removal patterns
Pitfall: iterating large arrays

Avoid attempting to process a very large list in a single transaction; it can fail as arrays grow.

// Swap and pop removal pattern
function removeFromOwner(uint256 index) internal {
    uint256 last = ownerAssets[msg.sender].length - 1;
    if (index != last) {
        ownerAssets[msg.sender][index] = ownerAssets[msg.sender][last];
    }
    ownerAssets[msg.sender].pop();
}
Tip

Keep an id-to-index mapping if you must remove specific elements frequently to avoid scanning for the index.

Off-chain indexing

Emit events and let off-chain services construct lists and histories, keeping on-chain operations minimal and cheap.

Warning

Do not rely on on-chain iteration for growing datasets; design for batching or off-chain queries to avoid gas failure.

screens.title: Testing and Remix workflow
screens.subtitle: Compile, deploy, and interact with ProductCatalog and AssetTracker

narration.text: The chapter's hands-on activity is designed for Remix. Begin by creating a new file and pasting the AssetTracker contract code. Compile using the Solidity compiler and choose a recent 0.8. x version. Deploy to JavaScript VM so you can rapidly iterate. In the deployed instance, call createAsset with a name to create two assets from the same account and then call getMyAssets to verify you see the expected array of IDs. Inspect each asset via assets(id) to verify owner and creation timestamp. To test transfer rules, switch to a second account, attempt to transfer and observe the require failure, then switch back to the owner and call transferAsset to move ownership to account two. Finally verify that getMyAssets reflects the new owners lists as described in the exercise — remembering the simplified demo may still have the old owner's id unless you implement removal. Use emitted events to confirm operations in the logs, and consider writing small unit tests to assert behaviors like require checks. Takeaway: the Remix loop of edit, compile, deploy, interact is the fastest way to validate your mapping, struct, and array logic and to observe storage versus memory behavior in practice.

screens.title: Design question and reasoning
screens.subtitle: Choose the best structure for a user profile registry

narration.text: The chapter provides an assessment question about storing user profiles with a numeric user ID mapped to a complex profile containing name, wallet, and reputation. The correct architecture is a mapping from the numeric ID to a UserProfile struct. The reasoning is that the struct groups related user fields into a single type and the mapping provides direct, efficient lookup by ID without scanning. A competing approach would be to store profiles in a dynamic array, but this requires iteration to find a specific ID and thus is inefficient for lookups. Another incorrect design scatters related fields across multiple mappings which complicates retrieval and increases the risk of inconsistency. When answering such design questions, weigh lookup patterns, iteration needs, and gas costs. If you need to produce a list of all users, maintain a separate array of user IDs for iteration or rely on events and off-chain indexing. Takeaway: prefer mapping plus struct for direct ID-to-profile storage and add an array of IDs only when you need enumerable lists, being mindful of the write cost. Design question and reasoning means for direct lookup of complex profiles by id, mapping to a struct is the most efficient and consistent pattern.. In practical terms, choose the best structure for a user profile registry. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Assessment insight
keyIdea.text: For direct lookup of complex profiles by ID, mapping to a struct is the most efficient and consistent pattern.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Design question and reasoning
Question

Store user profiles and allow fast lookup by ID

Which combo best stores profiles containing name, wallet, and reputation for direct lookup by numeric ID?

// Correct pattern
struct UserProfile {
    string name;
    address wallet;
    uint256 reputation;
}
mapping(uint256 => UserProfile) public profiles;
Why mapping + struct
  • Direct lookup by id is O(1).
  • Struct groups related fields for atomic reads and writes.
  • Maintains a single source of truth and reduces inconsistency.
Key Takeaway

Mapping from id to a struct is the most efficient, clear, and consistent choice when you need direct profile lookup by ID.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential concepts from this chapter

narration.text: Let's close with three compact reminders you should keep in mind. First, mappings are the fast, non-iterable key-value stores you will use for direct lookups such as balances or ownership. Second, structs let you group related fields into a single record, which simplifies storage and access patterns; be explicit about storage or memory when you read or modify them. Third, arrays enable ordered collections and iteration, but they come with gas trade-offs for large datasets and deletions. Use events and off-chain indexing when on-chain enumeration would be too expensive. Together, mapping plus struct plus array forms a practical pattern for registries and asset trackers, but always minimize duplicated state and plan removal strategies. Keep these three ideas as a checklist when designing or reviewing contracts. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts
Mapping
A key-value store for O(1) lookups. Keys are not enumerable; pair with arrays for iteration.
Struct
Group related fields into a single type. Use storage for persistent edits and memory for temporary copies.
Array
Ordered collection with push, pop, and length. Avoid full-array loops; use swap-pop for removals.
Final summary

Design contracts that use mapping for truth, structs for modeling, and arrays or events for listing while minimizing redundant state and gas-costly operations.

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders close as you code. First, always ask whether you need enumeration; if not, mappings are the best choice for lookup speed. Second, prefer a single source of truth: store the entity in a mapping to avoid duplicating fields across multiple structures. Third, plan for growth: use events and off-chain indexing for large datasets, and adopt swap-and-pop or index mappings for efficient removals. These small rules help you design contracts that scale, are easier to test, and cost less to operate on-chain. Ask yourself after each feature: where will the data be read, who will write it, and how often will lists grow?
